title: Yajña: The Spirit of Seva
subtitle: The Art of Giving: Harmonising Heart, Head and Hands
when_where: NZICA Wellness Retreat, Sunday 15 November 2026, Vedanta Retreat Centre, Glen Murray, and on Zoom. Session 1, talk by Swami Tadananda, Ramakrishna Vedanta Centre NZ.

quiz.desc: Twenty-five question quiz on Yajña: The Spirit of Seva, the talk at the NZICA Wellness Retreat, Ramakrishna Vedanta Centre NZ. It asks you to understand and apply the teaching.
quiz.og_title: Quiz: Yajña, the Spirit of Seva
quiz.og_desc: Twenty-five questions that ask you to understand and apply the teaching on yajña and seva.
quiz.blessing: May all your work become an offering, for the good of many and the joy of many.

questions.q: Two members each give four hours a month to their branch. After three years one has grown calmer, kinder and less easily hurt; the other is tired and quietly resentful. What does the teaching on yajña see as the deciding difference?
o: The inner attitude: one offers the work and lets go of “I and mine”, the other works for return or from pressure.
The kind of work each was given, since some tasks are naturally far more uplifting to do than others.
Their natural temperament, because service can only bring out more clearly what was already in a person.
The thanks each one received, since warm appreciation from others is what keeps any volunteer growing over the years.
questions.e: The Gītā says that work done for any purpose other than yajña binds us, while work offered as yajña sets us free (3.9). The same four hours can bind one person and purify another, because the difference lies in the attitude, not in the hours. The other options hold some truth: tasks differ, temperaments differ, thanks is pleasant. But none of them decides whether service becomes growth. Only the spirit of offering does that, and it is in our own hands.
questions.r: After my last piece of service, did I feel lighter or heavier, and what was I holding on to?

questions.q: Four members explain why they joined NZICA. Which one has most fully understood the motto ātmano mokṣārthaṁ jagad-hitāya ca, “for one’s own liberation and for the welfare of the world”?
o: “I come to serve the community. My spiritual life is a separate, private matter that I keep at home.”
“I come mainly for my own peace of mind. Helping others is a pleasant extra that comes along with it.”
“First I must become pure and wise myself. Only once I have reached that point will I begin serving others.”
“Serving with the right attitude purifies my mind, and a purer mind serves better; each helps the other.”
questions.e: The small word ca, “and”, joins the two aims into one path. To grow means to expand from the small self to the larger Self; to serve is to acknowledge our oneness with all. Each of the other three members has kept one half and lost the other: service without inner growth, growth without real service, or growth postponed until some future day. Swami Vivekananda’s ideal is that we grow through serving and serve better as we grow.
questions.r: Where in my life do I keep “my spiritual practice” and “my service” in separate boxes?

questions.q: After a year of regular seva, how could a member best tell whether it has become spiritual growth and not just more activity?
o: By the number of hours worked, events organised and people served, all carefully recorded over the year.
By the appreciation and recognition received from the community and from the leaders of the association.
By Swami Ranganathananda’s test: more oneness with others, more inner peace, and that peace radiating around, even in hard moments.
By a growing certainty that one’s own way of serving is the right one, and that others should follow it.
questions.e: Swami Ranganathananda asked: Are you growing spiritually? Can you feel oneness with others? Have you peace within yourself? And do you radiate it around you? These are signs of character, not of activity. Hours and events can grow while the ego grows with them; recognition is a return, not a sign of growth; and certainty that others should follow our way is often ego in a new form.
questions.r: Over the past year, has my peace grown, and do the people around me feel it?

questions.q: Arjun says: “I have worked hard for everything I have. I owe nothing to anyone.” His hard work is real. What does the wheel of yajña (Gītā 3.14 to 3.16) show that his view leaves out?
o: That effort counts for very little in the end, because every result is already decided by fate and the devas.
That he should give generously now, so that good fortune and success keep flowing back to him in all the years ahead.
That his effort rests on countless gifts he never earned, so giving back completes the circle rather than being charity.
That he owes a fixed debt to society which he can repay in full once and then consider closed for good.
questions.e: The Gītā describes life as a wheel: beings live on food, food comes from rain, rain from yajña, and yajña from action (3.14). Arjun’s effort stands on the gifts of parents, teachers, the land, the rain and the community. Seeing this does not cancel his effort; it places it inside a larger circle of giving. The wrong options turn the teaching into fatalism, into a business deal, or into a debt that can be paid off and forgotten. Gratitude is not a bill; it is a way of living.
questions.r: List five things I received this week without paying for them. What would giving back look like?

questions.q: After reading that one who enjoys life’s gifts without giving is “a thief” (3.12), Maya becomes anxious and guilty, and gives out of fear that she is never doing enough. Which advice would help her most?
o: She should work out roughly what she has received over the years and give back that amount, so the account is settled.
The word is meant to awaken gratitude, not fear. Giving that flows from gratitude frees the mind; giving from guilt keeps it anxious.
Her anxiety shows she is taking the verse seriously, so she should keep increasing her giving until the guilt goes away.
She should set the verse aside, since a teaching first given for ancient fire rituals does not really apply to modern life.
questions.e: Strong words in scripture are meant to wake us, not to frighten us. When giving comes from fear or guilt, the mind stays centred on itself: “Am I good enough?” When it comes from gratitude, the mind turns outward and becomes light. Exact accounting misses the spirit, more giving will not cure guilt, and setting the verse aside throws away a teaching that still applies to every one of us.
questions.r: Does my giving come more from gratitude or from a sense of obligation? How does each one feel inside?

questions.q: A busy family rarely eats together, and the teenagers find religious customs dull. Which first step would best bring the spirit of Gītā 3.13, sharing food as prasāda, into this home?
o: Print verse 3.13 in Sanskrit and put it on the fridge, so that everyone in the family sees it every single day.
Cook more elaborate meals at the weekend, so that the family learns to value food and the time spent eating it.
Let each person say a private prayer before eating, whenever they eat, so that no one feels the practice is forced.
Once a week, pause together before a shared meal to remember where the food came from, offer it, then share it.
questions.e: Verse 3.13 says that those who eat what remains after offering are freed from faults, while those who cook only for themselves eat sin. The point is a change of attitude: food becomes a gift received and shared. A small, regular, shared pause does this best, and it can grow. A verse on the fridge informs but does not transform. Better food may please without changing the attitude. Private prayer is good, but the verse is about sharing.
questions.r: Can I pause before my next meal to remember the many hands that brought it to me?

questions.q: At a food drive Raj thinks: “I am the one helping these poor people.” He works hard and means well. What is the hidden error in his feeling, and what corrects it at the root?
o: He is helping too few people; reaching many more would gradually turn his pride into real and lasting compassion.
He uses the word “poor”; if he simply chose kinder words, the problem in his attitude would disappear by itself.
He sees himself as the high giver and them as low receivers; seeing all as one Reality (4.24) turns pride into gratitude.
He is enjoying the work too much; real service should feel like a hard duty, carried out without taking any pleasure in it at all.
questions.e: Brahmārpaṇam (4.24): the offering, the fire, the one who offers and the act of offering are all Brahman. Raj’s error is the line he draws between himself and those he serves. Numbers, words and feelings of enjoyment are all on the surface. When he sees the Divine in each person, pride gives way to reverence, and, as Swami Vivekananda taught, he will feel grateful to them for the chance to serve.
questions.r: Whom do I sometimes look down on, even slightly, while I help them?

questions.q: Mohan says: “Swami Vivekananda called image worship only preliminary, so I have stopped my shrine worship and use that time to volunteer.” How should we evaluate his decision?
o: He is right, because real worship is service, and time at the shrine is time taken away from people in need.
He has misread the teaching: a beginning is meant to grow, not to be discarded. Worship and service nourish each other.
He is right only if he is a monk; householders should keep worship at home and leave service to the Mission.
He is wrong, because service is only a preparation, and the real worship happens before the sacred image in the family shrine.
questions.e: “He who sees Shiva in the poor, in the weak, and in the diseased, really worships Shiva; and if he sees Shiva only in the image, his worship is but preliminary.” Preliminary means a first step, not a mistake. The love and remembrance practised at the shrine are what let us see the same Divine in people. As Swami Ranganathananda put it, spiritual growth comes from meditation inwardly and service outwardly. Mohan has cut one of the two wings.
questions.r: How does my time of worship or meditation show itself in the way I serve, and the other way round?

questions.q: A coordinator notices that some helpers at a community pantry speak down to the guests. Bringing together “the giver is blessed” and serving the living God in people, which change would address this at the root?
o: Help the helpers see each visit as a privilege: greet and thank every guest, serve with respect, and remember who is blessed.
Make a firm rule that helpers say no more to the guests than is needed, so that hurtful remarks are simply prevented.
Award helpers a badge for every month of service, so that they feel valued themselves and become more generous.
Move the service to home delivery, so that guests and helpers no longer meet and there is no chance of disrespect.
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda said: “It is not the receiver that is blessed, but it is the giver.” He called it a great privilege to be allowed to worship God by helping our fellow-man. The other changes manage the symptom: silence, rewards and distance do not change how helpers see the guests. Only a change of vision, learned together and practised at every visit, removes the root.
questions.r: When I last helped someone, did I feel that I was doing them a favour, or that they were doing me one?

questions.q: Read each person’s inner attitude. Which step on the ladder of purification best describes where each one stands now? Choose one for each line.
rows: Arun gladly takes on a committee role, but feels let down when his name is left off the thank-you list.
Meena gives quietly every week and is untroubled whether anyone notices, because giving is simply right.
Hari inwardly says “This is for You” before each task, at work and at home, and takes the results as prasāda.
Lila, caring for a frail elder, feels no separation between herself, the care and the one she cares for.
questions.e: Arun is giving for a return, here recognition (rājasika, 17.12); notice that the sign is not the act but the disappointment. Meena gives because it is right, seeking nothing (sāttvika, 17.11). Hari offers all his work to the Lord (9.27). Lila sees giver, gift and receiver as one Reality (4.24). Each step loosens “I and mine” a little more, and the same person may stand on different steps on different days.
questions.r: Which person is most like me today, and what one change would lift me to the next step?

questions.q: Anita is a retired teacher who lives alone on a small pension. She says: “I have no money, so I cannot really do seva.” Which plan best fits the teaching on the many forms of yajña?
o: Save a little each week until she can make one sizeable donation, since material giving is the clearest form of seva.
Accept that her years of seva have passed, and support those who still can with her good wishes and her thanks.
Offer what she has: help children of new families with reading, and pray for others daily. Both are yajña.
Join the busiest committee she can find, since only public, organised work really counts as service to the community.
questions.e: The Gītā lists many offerings: of wealth, of discipline, of study and knowledge (4.25 to 4.30). Swami Vivekananda spoke of physical, intellectual and spiritual help, and called the gift of knowledge “a far higher gift than that of food and clothes”. Anita’s years as a teacher are a treasure to offer, and prayer for others is itself an offering. The other plans assume that only money or public work counts, or that age closes the door.
questions.r: What is my particular gift to offer: time, skill, knowledge, care or prayer?

questions.q: Ashok says: “Charity begins at home. I will care for my family now, and serve the community later, when the children have grown up.” In the light of the five daily offerings and the widening circles, how should we evaluate this?
o: He is right, because duty to the family must come first, and the wider circles can wait until that duty is done.
The family is the first field of seva, but the circles widen together. Small offerings to others can start now and teach the children.
He is wrong, because attachment to family is a form of “mine” and has to be given up for selfless public service.
Only the widest circle, service to all beings, counts as real yajña, since caring for one’s own is never selfless.
questions.e: The pañca mahāyajña, the five daily offerings, widen our care step by step from the self to all beings, and every householder practises them every day, not one after another over a lifetime. Caring for children and elders is truly yajña. But when the wider circles are postponed, the children learn that care stops at the front door. Children learn seva by seeing it. Despising family duty, or calling it never selfless, misses that the home is the first circle.
questions.r: Which circle of my care is the narrowest right now, and how could I widen it a little this month?

questions.q: Vikram works hard at every event, but afterwards he complains about the organisers to anyone who will listen. In terms of yajña in thought, word and deed, where is his offering incomplete, and why does it matter for him?
o: In word and thought: his hands offer, but his speech and mind still grasp, so resentment undoes the purification.
In deed: if he did even more work at each event, there would be no time left for the complaints to arise.
Nowhere at all: what counts is the help actually given, and private complaints do not affect the service itself in any way.
In leadership: he should ask for a role on the committee, so that he can put right the things that annoy him.
questions.e: Our spiritual tradition speaks of purity manasā, vācā, karmaṇā: in thought, word and deed. Vikram’s deeds are an offering, but his words and thoughts take back what his hands gave. The work could purify his mind, yet resentment keeps feeding “I and mine”. More work only adds fatigue, saying it does not matter ignores the effect on him and on others, and a committee role would give the same grasping a larger stage.
questions.r: In which of the three, thought, word or deed, do I most often take back what I have given?

questions.q: Swami Vivekananda taught that real service needs heart, head and hands in harmony. In each case, what is missing? Choose one for each line.
rows: Ravi designs an efficient roster for the meals service, but treats both volunteers and guests as names on a sheet.
Shanti is moved to tears by a family’s hardship and rushes to give whatever comes to mind, though it is not what they need.
Mahesh feels for the lonely elders and has a clear plan for weekly visits, but each week something else comes first.
Uma notices a newcomer struggling, finds out what she really needs, and quietly helps her settle in over several weeks.
c: Heart, head and hands are in harmony
questions.e: Ravi has head and hands but no heart, so his service becomes cold. Shanti has heart and hands but no head, so her help misses the real need. Mahesh has heart and head but no hands, so nothing happens. Uma shows all three together: she feels, she understands the real need, and she carries it through. Heart alone becomes sentimental, head alone becomes cold, hands alone become tiring. Together, giving becomes an art.
questions.r: In my own service, which is weakest: heart, head or hands? What would strengthen it?

questions.q: Kiran hears that we should be “merely an instrument” of the Divine and concludes: “Then the results are up to God, so it does not matter much how carefully I prepare.” How should we evaluate his reasoning?
o: He is right: an instrument has no responsibility of its own, so careful preparation would only feed the ego of the doer.
He is right about results but wrong about effort, since effort is what earns us a good result from the Lord in return.
He has misunderstood: being an instrument is a state reserved for saints, and ordinary members should simply work hard.
He has turned it upside down: an instrument must be well tuned. Give full skill and care, and let go only of “I am the doer” and anxiety.
questions.e: Gītā 2.50 says yoga is skill in action, and Sri Ramakrishna prayed, “O Mother, Thou art the Operator and I am the machine.” A machine the Operator can use well is clean, oiled and in good order. Being an instrument removes the ego and the anxiety, not the care. The second option turns offering into a bargain; the third puts the ideal out of reach, though every sevak can begin to practise it in small things today.
questions.r: In which task do I use “it is all God’s will” as a reason to give less than my best?

questions.q: Leela gives a large donation anonymously, but each month she checks the newsletter and feels a little let down that no one has guessed it was her. How would the Gītā’s teaching on sāttvika giving (17.20) assess this, and what is the way forward?
o: Fully sāttvika, because only the anonymous act itself counts, not the passing feelings that come up afterwards.
Of no spiritual value, since a gift mixed with any wish for credit is spoiled, so she should stop until her motive is pure.
Outwardly sāttvika, inwardly still seeking a return. Keep giving, notice the wish kindly and offer it too.
Tāmasika, because giving in secret lacks the honesty and openness of a gift that is made plainly in public.
questions.e: The Gītā calls a gift sāttvika when it is given because it is right to give, to a worthy cause, at the right time, expecting nothing in return (17.20). Leela’s act meets this outwardly, but a quiet wish for credit remains. That is how purification usually works: the act comes first and the motive is refined by practice. Calling it already perfect stops her growth; calling it worthless would stop the giving that is purifying her. Secrecy is not tamas.
questions.r: When I give, what small return am I still hoping for, and can I offer that too?

questions.q: Two branches keep competing to hold the bigger Diwali event, and members of each speak a little scornfully of the other. What is really happening, according to the teaching on “I and mine”?
o: This is healthy competition, which spurs both branches on to do more good, so nothing needs to change here.
The ego has not gone; it has widened to “my branch”. The cure is to see both as offerings to one fire.
There are simply too many events; if each branch held fewer, the rivalry between them would fade by itself.
The fault lies mainly with whichever branch began the rivalry, so it is up to that branch to make the first move.
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda taught that the whole secret of unselfish work is giving up “I and mine”. Ego can hide inside good work: “my branch, my event, my success”. A wider “mine” is still “mine”. When both branches see their events as offerings into one sacred fire, each can rejoice in the other’s success. Fewer events, blame, or calling it healthy competition all leave the root untouched.
questions.r: Where has my “I and mine” quietly grown to include my group, my family or my branch?

questions.q: In a committee meeting Neha is criticised unfairly for a project she leads. Drawing on Gītā 12.13 (free from “mine” and ego, forgiving, even in pain and pleasure) and the idea that the work is the Lord’s, which response shows these qualities growing?
o: She listens calmly, corrects anything true, lets go of the hurt and bears no grudge: the work is not hers to defend.
She resigns quietly from the project, since a sevak should avoid all conflict and never stand in another’s way.
She defends herself firmly, to protect the good name of the project and of everyone who has worked hard on it.
She agrees outwardly but avoids that member afterwards, so that peace is kept without any open argument.
questions.e: Verse 12.13 describes one who “hates no being, is friendly and compassionate to all, free from ‘mine’ and from ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving”. If the project is an offering, criticism does not have to wound the ego, and any truth in it can be used. Resigning, defending or quiet avoidance can each look wise, but each is still about protecting “I”. Forgiveness here is not weakness; it is freedom.
questions.r: When I am criticised, what am I really trying to protect?

questions.q: Deepak skipped his morning prayer for months so that he could start volunteering earlier. He is now efficient but often irritable. Combining Swami Ranganathananda’s teaching (meditation inwardly, service outwardly) and the sevak’s day, what would restore balance?
o: Take a month off from all service to meditate full time, and then come back to the work once he feels calm again.
Carry on just as he is, since service is itself a kind of meditation and the irritation will settle down in time.
Volunteer fewer hours but keep the same morning routine, since tiredness alone is what is causing the irritation.
Keep a short, fixed time of meditation or japa before work, and brief remembrance during it, so service is fed from within.
questions.e: Swami Ranganathananda taught that spiritual growth is stimulated by meditation inwardly and by work done in a spirit of service outwardly. The sevak’s day begins by filling the cup before pouring it out. Deepak’s irritability shows the inner source running dry. A month away swings to the other extreme, carrying on ignores the warning, and cutting hours treats only the tiredness. A small daily balance of both is the way.
questions.r: Is my cup being filled each day as well as poured out? What fills it?

questions.q: Sunita is a nurse working long shifts. She feels guilty that she has “no time left for seva”. How does work as worship (Gītā 2.50 and 9.27) apply to her?
o: Her nursing, done with skill, care and inner offering, is itself seva; brief remembrance between patients makes her shift a yajña.
Her work is paid, so it cannot count as seva; she must find some unpaid hours each week for her real service.
She should cut her hours at the hospital, since service to the community matters more than her career.
Her work counts as seva only when she cares for patients who come from her own cultural community.
questions.e: “Yoga is skill in action” (2.50), and “Whatever you do, do it as an offering to Me” (9.27). A sevak is not only someone who volunteers at weekends; for a sevak the whole day becomes one yajña. Payment does not stop work from being an offering, and the Divine in each patient is the same. Sunita needs a change of attitude, not of job.
questions.r: Which part of my daily work could become an offering, without changing anything outwardly?

questions.q: At his evening review Rohan notices that he was impatient twice during the day. In the spirit of the sevak’s evening offering, what should he do with this?
o: Make up for it by fasting or doing extra service the next day, so that the fault is properly paid for.
Note it honestly, offer it with the day’s work to the Lord, resolve gently to do better, and rest without self-condemnation.
Think only of what went well, since dwelling on faults weakens confidence and the will to serve others.
Write each fault in detail and read the list every morning, so that he stays humble and does not forget.
questions.e: The evening offering asks two gentle questions: Where did I serve? Where did “I and mine” creep in? Then everything, success and failure alike, is offered to the Lord. Holy Mother’s counsel was to look at one’s own faults rather than at the faults of others, and to do so with love, not harshness. Punishment, denial and a list of faults all keep the mind circling around the small self; honest seeing with offering lets it grow.
questions.r: Tonight, can I look back on my day honestly, and then let it go into the Lord’s hands?

questions.q: Dev gave years to his branch committee. When he is not re-elected he feels he has lost himself, and he stops coming. In the light of “Who are we?”, what has really happened?
o: He took a role for his identity; the “unripe I” of position was hurt. His true Self is untouched, and he can still serve as a member.
He was treated unfairly, and his hurt shows how much he cared; the branch should give him back a title to make amends.
He has learned that committee work brings only disappointment in the end, so it is wiser for him to step back quietly from community life now.
He was attached to the work itself, so the healthiest choice is to stop serving altogether until the attachment fades.
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda: “Each soul is potentially divine.” We are not our roles, titles or possessions. Sri Ramakrishna taught that the “unripe I” says “my position, my group”, while the “ripe I” says “I am the servant of God”. Dev’s pain shows where he had placed his identity. The remedy is not a new title, nor withdrawal, but to remember who he is and offer what he can, with or without a role. Nothing real has been taken from him.
questions.r: Which role or title do I quietly treat as who I am?

questions.q: A branch is planning Diwali. Some elders want every detail done exactly as in their home town; several young members find parts of it meaningless and are drifting away. Bringing together the test for what to protect and what to let go, and “each took up their own share”, what is the wisest way forward?
o: Do everything exactly as before, since our heritage is precious and changing any part of it means losing it for good.
Keep and explain the heart of the festival, its light, prayer and sharing, and let the young help shape the form so it becomes theirs too.
Let the young members design a modern event of their own, since the old customs mean little in Aotearoa now.
Hold two separate events, one traditional and one modern, so that each group can celebrate fully in its own way and no one feels pushed aside.
questions.e: The test is whether something helps us grow in love, truth and unselfishness. The meaning of Diwali, the victory of light within, passes that test and must be protected and passed on, in ways the young can love and understand. Some outer forms may have lost their meaning for this generation. The Saṁjñāna Sūkta asks for one purpose with each taking up their own share. Freezing every detail, discarding the heritage, or splitting the community all fail the test of unity.
questions.r: Which custom in my family or branch needs its meaning explained, and which one needs to be let go?

questions.q: NZICA wants its branches to work together on one national project. Which approach best embodies the Saṁjñāna Sūkta, “walk together, speak together, let your minds be of one accord”, and the image of many offerings into one fire?
o: The national office designs every detail, and every branch carries out the same tasks, so that unity is ensured.
Each branch picks its own separate project, so that freedom is respected and no branch is pushed by any other.
Agree together on one purpose, let each branch give its own share by its strengths, and celebrate jointly.
The largest branch leads and the others support it, since one strong centre avoids confusion and wasted effort.
questions.e: Ṛg Veda 10.191 asks for a common purpose, a common assembly and a common mind, and the devas each take up their share. Unity is not sameness, and freedom is not separateness. In one sacred fire, each offering is different, yet all rise as one flame. Central control loses the gifts of the branches; separate projects lose the common purpose; a single dominant branch loses the equality the hymn asks for.
questions.r: What is my branch’s particular share to offer to the whole of NZICA?

questions.q: Six months after the retreat, Priya, who heard the talk, read the paper and scored well on the quiz, notices that nothing in her daily life has changed. Which next step best reflects śravaṇa, manana, nididhyāsana and Swami Vivekananda’s idea of assimilation?
o: Read the study paper again and retake the quiz until she gets full marks, so that the ideas are firmly in place.
Attend more talks on other topics, so that a wider range of knowledge gradually leads to some change in her life.
Accept that this path does not suit her nature, and look for a different spiritual practice that will work better.
Choose one idea, such as offering each morning’s work, live it daily until it is natural, then take up another.
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda said: “If you have assimilated five ideas and made them your life and character, you have more education than any man who has got by heart a whole library.” Śravaṇa is hearing, manana is reflection, and nididhyāsana is living the idea until it becomes part of us. Priya has done the first two. More reading, more talks or a new path all stay at the level of information; one idea lived daily is what changes character.
questions.r: Which one idea from this study will I make part of my life, starting tomorrow?

cms.intro: Yajña, life lived as an offering, is the spirit of seva. This talk from the NZICA Wellness Retreat, The Art of Giving, shows how serving others with the right attitude purifies our own minds and hearts, and how many members giving together become a powerful force for the good of many. Study the slides, read the study paper slowly, then reflect with the quiz.
cms.summary: Yajña, life lived as an offering, is the spirit of seva. Starting from the two reasons people join a community, to grow and to serve, the talk shows they are one path. It explores the Bhagavad Gītā’s wheel of giving and receiving, the Divine in every part of the offering, how yajña purifies mind and heart, the many forms of yajña, the quality of our offering, and a day in the life of a sevak as one continuous yajña. It answers NZICA’s three questions: why volunteer for community work, what a day looks like in the life of a person dedicated to seva, and who we are, what to protect and what needs to go. Along the way it shows how heart, head and hands, offered together, make the whole person an instrument of the Divine. It closes with the collective yajña of an association: many offerings, one sacred fire, for the good of many and the joy of many.
reflection_questions: Why did I join NZICA, and how are my reasons to grow and to serve connected?
What have I received this week without paying for it, and what could I give back?
On which step of the ladder of purification do I usually stand when I serve?
Which part of my day could become an offering tomorrow?
In my service, which is weakest: heart, head or hands?
What in my life, family or branch must be protected, and what needs to go?
What is my branch’s particular share to offer to the whole of NZICA?
suggested_reading: Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda: Karma-Yoga
Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda: Address at the Rameswaram Temple on Real Worship
The study paper Yajña: The Spirit of Seva (RET-001)

on: The session title with both emblems, the Ramakrishna Vedanta Centre NZ and the NZ Indian Central Association, over an aerial view of the Vedanta Retreat Centre at Glen Murray.

paras: Welcome everyone, in the hall and on Zoom. Session 1 runs from 8:30 to 10:00 am: the lighting of the lamps, welcomes, the talk on the art of giving, seva stories, questions, and the seva tree before tea.

on: The prayer asato mā sad gamaya, chanted while the lamps are lit jointly.

vs.dev:
असतो मा सद्गमय ।
तमसो मा ज्योतिर्गमय ।
मृत्योर्मा अमृतं गमय ॥
vs.iast:
asato mā sad gamaya, tamaso mā jyotir gamaya,
mṛtyor mā amṛtaṁ gamaya
vs.en: Lead me from the unreal to the Real, from darkness to Light, from death to Immortality.

paras: The lamps are lit jointly. We chant this prayer together while the lamps are lit: the outer light as a symbol of the inner light we seek, and the light of knowledge we hope to share with others.

on: Welcomes from Veer Khar, President of the NZ Indian Central Association, and Shefali Mehta, Chair of the NZICA Health and Wellness Sub-Committee.

paras: About three minutes each. Veer first, then Shefali.

on: The first verse of the Saṁjñāna Sūkta in Devanagari and transliteration, with the meaning of each word, for all to read and chant together.

vs.dev:
सं गच्छध्वं सं वदध्वं सं वो मनांसि जानताम् ।
देवा भागं यथा पूर्वे संजानाना उपासते ॥
vs.iast:
saṁ gacchadhvaṁ saṁ vadadhvaṁ saṁ vo manāṁsi jānatām,
devā bhāgaṁ yathā pūrve saṁjānānā upāsate.
vs.en: Walk together, speak together, let your minds know one another, as the devas of old, in harmony, each took up their own share.

paras: The theme of the whole day: the Saṁjñāna Sūkta, the hymn of harmony that closes the Rig Veda. Invite everyone, in the hall and on Zoom, to read and repeat each line after you, slowly, twice. Point to the word cards: saṁ, together, repeats three times in the first line: together in walking (action), in speaking (words) and in knowing (minds). "Each took up their own share": unity is not sameness; each person and each branch offers its own gifts to the common purpose.

on: The second verse with word meanings. A gold card links it to the day: our seva together is the common offering.

vs.dev:
समानो मन्त्रः समितिः समानी समानं मनः सह चित्तमेषाम् ।
समानं मन्त्रमभि मन्त्रये वः समानेन वो हविषा जुहोमि ॥
vs.iast:
samāno mantraḥ samitiḥ samānī samānaṁ manaḥ saha cittam eṣām,
samānaṁ mantram abhi mantraye vaḥ samānena vo haviṣā juhomi.
vs.en: Common be your counsel, one your assembly, alike your minds, joined your thoughts. I place before you a common purpose, and worship with your common offering.

gl: the offering poured into the sacred fire

paras: Read and repeat. A shared purpose (mantra), a shared gathering (samiti), minds and hearts joined (manas, citta), and a shared offering (havis). In the Vedic fire ritual, everyone's offering goes into one fire. Our seva together is that common offering.

on: The third verse with word meanings, closing with Om śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ.

vs.dev:
समानी व आकूतिः समाना हृदयानि वः ।
समानमस्तु वो मनो यथा वः सुसहासति ॥
vs.iast:
samānī va ākūtiḥ samānā hṛdayāni vaḥ,
samānam astu vo mano yathā vaḥ susahāsati.
vs.en: One be your intention, united your hearts, one your mind, so that you may live and work happily together.

paras: Read and repeat, then close with Om śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ. Four words to carry through the day: ākūti, intention (why did I come?); manas, mind (how do I think?); hṛdaya, heart (how do I feel toward others?); bhāga, share (what part do I offer?). Su-saha: su, well; saha, together. We will chant the whole hymn again at the close of the retreat.

on: The title of Swami Tadananda’s talk: growing through giving, for ourselves and for the good of many.

paras: About 40 minutes. The central idea: yajña, life lived as an offering, is the spirit of seva. At the individual level it purifies the mind and heart so the inner light shines through; when many minds offer together, bahujana hitāya bahujana sukhāya, the association becomes a powerful force for collective good. A day in the life of a sevak is one continuous yajña.

on: NZICA’s three questions for the retreat, each answered by yajña: why volunteer for community work; a day in the life of a person dedicated to seva; who are we, what to protect and what needs to go.

paras: When NZICA invited us, the Association suggested three questions: why volunteer for community work; what a day looks like in the life of a person dedicated to seva; and who are we, what do we need to protect and what needs to go. This talk answers all three with one idea from the Bhagavad Gītā, yajña, life lived as an offering, and with the title of our retreat: harmonising heart, head and hands, so that the whole person becomes an instrument of the Divine.

on: Two cards, To grow and To serve, each with its half of the motto ātmano mokṣārthaṁ jagad-hitāya ca.

vs.en: For one’s own liberation, and for the welfare of the world.

paras: Invite a show of hands: who joined mainly to grow? Mainly to serve? Both? Then reveal that these two reasons are the two halves of the motto Swami Vivekananda gave the Ramakrishna Order, which the Vedanta Centre follows. To grow (ātmano mokṣārtham) means expansion: the small self opening into the larger Self, becoming unselfish, manifesting the divinity within. To serve (jagad-hitāya ca) means acknowledging our oneness with everyone: we are all waves of the same ocean, so in serving others we serve our own universal higher Self, the Paramātman. The small word "ca", "and", joins them: the more we grow, the more naturally we serve; the more we serve, the more we grow. The next slides unfold this through the two pillars of Vedanta and the waves and the ocean.

slides.t: Serving the living God, we grow
on: Swami Vivekananda on the privilege of serving God in man; Swami Ranganathananda’s question, Are you growing spiritually?; and meditation and service as partners.

paras: Swami Vivekananda called service a privilege: we are allowed to worship the living God, present in every human being. In his letter of 1897 he goes further: he would gladly be born again and again to worship "the only God that exists, the sum total of all souls". Swami Ranganathananda, the 13th President of the Ramakrishna Math and Mission, gives us a simple test of spiritual growth in four questions: Are you growing spiritually? Can you feel oneness with others? Have you peace within yourself? And do you radiate it around you? He adds that this growth is stimulated by meditation inwardly and by work done in a spirit of service outwardly. That is exactly the band across the bottom of this slide: meditation and service go together like two wings of a bird. Meditation turns the wave toward the ocean within; service lets it see the ocean in every other wave. Please check the full wording of the 1897 letter in Complete Works Vol. 5 before the retreat.

on: The divinity of the soul and the oneness of existence, with what each means for the person who serves.

vs.dev:
यस्तु सर्वाणि भूतान्यात्मन्येवानुपश्यति ।
सर्वभूतेषु चात्मानं ततो न विजुगुप्सते ॥
vs.iast:
yas tu sarvāṇi bhūtāny ātmany evānupaśyati,
sarva-bhūteṣu cātmānaṁ tato na vijugupsate
vs.en: One who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, hates none.

paras: Everything in this talk rests on these two pillars. First: every soul is divine. The divinity is already there, only covered; life is the process of uncovering it. Second: existence is one. There is one Reality appearing as many. If these two are true, then serving another is worship (because they are divine), and serving another is serving myself (because we are one). Seva is not charity from above; it is worship and it is self-discovery.

on: A drawn ocean with waves of many sizes: the waves are each of us; the ocean is the one divine Reality, sat-cit-ānanda.

paras: Every wave looks separate. One is tall, one is small; one is rising, one is breaking on the shore. Yet every wave is made of the same water and rests on the same ocean. We are all different waves on the one ocean of the Divine. The small wave who thinks "I am only this little wave" feels limited, anxious and alone. The wave who knows "I am the ocean" feels infinite existence, knowledge and bliss: sat-cit-ānanda. Sat: existence that never ends. Cit: consciousness, knowledge. Ānanda: bliss, a joy that depends on nothing outside.

on: The three meanings of the root yaj, worship, coming together and giving, and how the Gītā widens yajña from the fire ritual to a way of life.

paras: The classical list of Sanskrit roots gives yaj three meanings: worship (deva-pūjā), coming together or association (saṅgati-karaṇa) and giving (dāna). All three belong to seva: when we give, we worship; when we come together to give, we become a living community. An association like NZICA is, in this sense, a yajña in itself. In Vedic times yajña was the fire ritual. Sri Krishna widens it in the Gītā: the fire may be the kitchen stove, the office desk, the hospital ward or the community hall; the offering may be time, skill, wealth, knowledge or simple care. In one sentence: yajña is life lived as an offering.

on: A diagram of two wheels: the wheel of yajña in the Gītā (3.14 to 3.16) and the same wheel turning in NZICA.

paras: Beings live on food, food comes from rain, rain from yajña, yajña from action, and Brahman is ever present in yajña (3.14, 3.15). Nothing in nature lives only for itself. The same wheel turns in an association: members offer time, skill and care; branch activities serve the community; the community is uplifted; trust grows and new members join and give in their turn. At the centre is one shared ideal: bahujana hitāya, the good of many. Verse 3.16: one who does not help turn the wheel lives in vain.

on: Gītā 3.12 and 3.13 in Devanagari with their meaning, and three cards: gratitude first, share the food, give back.

vs.dev:
इष्टान्भोगान्हि वो देवा दास्यन्ते यज्ञभाविताः ।
तैर्दत्तानप्रदायैभ्यो यो भुङ्क्ते स्तेन एव सः ॥
vs.iast:
iṣṭān bhogān hi vo devā dāsyante yajña-bhāvitāḥ,
tair dattān apradāyaibhyo yo bhuṅkte stena eva saḥ
vs.en: Nourished by yajña, the devas will give you the good things you desire. One who enjoys what they give without offering anything in return is nothing but a thief.

vs.dev:
यज्ञशिष्टाशिनः सन्तो मुच्यन्ते सर्वकिल्बिषैः ।
भुञ्जते ते त्वघं पापा ये पचन्त्यात्मकारणात् ॥
vs.iast:
yajña-śiṣṭāśinaḥ santo mucyante sarva-kilbiṣaiḥ,
bhuñjate te tv aghaṁ pāpā ye pacanty ātma-kāraṇāt
vs.en: The good who eat what remains after yajña are freed from all faults. But those who cook only for themselves eat sin.

gl: blessed food, what remains after offering

paras: Strong words from Sri Krishna, but the point is gratitude, not guilt. Each of us has received far more than we can count: from parents and teachers, from the land and its people, from those who came to Aotearoa before us and built the community we enjoy. Verse 3.13 is the origin of offering food before eating and sharing prasāda. Ask: what have I received this week without paying for it, and what could I give back? Giving back is our share in turning the wheel.

slides.t: The Divine in every part of the offering
on: Gītā 4.24, often chanted before meals, with four cards: the giver, the gift and the receiver are waves; all are one ocean.

vs.dev:
ब्रह्मार्पणं ब्रह्म हविर्ब्रह्माग्नौ ब्रह्मणा हुतम् ।
ब्रह्मैव तेन गन्तव्यं ब्रह्मकर्मसमाधिना ॥
vs.iast:
brahmārpaṇaṁ brahma havir brahmāgnau brahmaṇā hutam,
brahmaiva tena gantavyaṁ brahma-karma-samādhinā
vs.en: The act of offering is Brahman, the offering is Brahman, it is offered by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. One who sees Brahman in every action reaches Brahman alone.

paras: Chanted before meals in many homes and in the ashrams of the Ramakrishna Order. It brings together the two pillars: every part of the act is the one Brahman. Giver, gift and receiver are waves of the same ocean; in serving others we serve our own universal Self, the Paramātman. Suggest everyone chant this verse before meals for one week and notice what changes.

on: Swami Vivekananda at the Rameswaram temple: seeing Shiva in the poor, the weak and the diseased is real worship.

paras: Swami Vivekananda spoke these words in 1897 at the great Rameswaram temple, in a place of pilgrimage, to people who had come to worship the image. He did not belittle the image: worship there is a beginning, a preparation. The fulfilment is to see the same Shiva, the same Divine, living and suffering in human beings, and to serve them. This is the heart of the Ramakrishna Order's ideal of service: serving the Divine in human beings.

slides.t: Giver or receiver: who gains more?
on: Swami Vivekananda in Karma-Yoga: the giver is blessed; we owe everything to the one we help; the world as a moral gymnasium.

paras: This turns ordinary thinking upside down. We usually think the giver is doing a favour. Swami Vivekananda says the opposite: the one we serve gives us the chance to grow purer, more loving, less selfish. The world does not need our help as much as we need to give it. Hence gratitude: "Be grateful that the poor man is there, so that by making a gift to him you are able to help yourself." And: "we must work and constantly do good, because it is a blessing to ourselves. That is the only way we can become perfect."

on: A diagram of six steps, from living for “I and mine” to the inner light, each with its Gītā verse.

paras: This is how we grow through service. From living for I and mine (3.12, 3.16), to giving for a return (rājasika, 17.12), to giving because it is right (sāttvika, 17.11), to work as worship (9.27), to seeing Brahman in all (4.24), to the inner light: all action fulfilled in knowledge (4.33). Each offering loosens I and mine; the mind grows clear like a clean window, and the light that was always within shines through. Yajña, giving and austerity purify even the wise (18.5).

on: Six forms of yajña from Gītā 4.25 to 4.33 and 10.25, and the question: what is my particular offering?

paras: Sri Krishna lists many kinds of yajña in 4.25 to 4.30: wealth, austerity, yoga, study, knowledge, breath control, sense restraint. All purify. The yajña of knowledge is higher than any offering of material things (4.33), and among all yajñas the Lord is japa, the repetition of the holy name (10.25), which anyone can offer anywhere. Swami Vivekananda in Karma-Yoga speaks of the same ladder in the help we give: physical, then intellectual, then spiritual help, the highest. Each member has a particular gift to offer.

on: A diagram of widening circles of offering, from the self to all beings, beside the five daily offerings, pañca mahāyajña.

paras: Our spiritual tradition gives every householder five daily offerings: to the Divine (deva yajña), to the sages through study (ṛṣi yajña), to parents and ancestors (pitṛ yajña), to fellow human beings through service and hospitality (nṛ yajña), and to animals and nature (bhūta yajña). Each circle widens the self: from I to family, to our branch, to society, to all beings. NZICA work is nṛ yajña.

slides.t: Yajña in thought, word and deed
on: A diagram contrasting grasping and offering in thought, word and deed: manasā, vācā, karmaṇā.

paras: Manasā, vācā, karmaṇā. Yajña is not only what we do. Each moment offers the same choice: to grasp or to offer. Thought: what do I get, or how can I help? Word: gossip and criticism, or truthful, kind, encouraging speech. Deed: taking without giving, or work done as worship. Invite members to notice which of the three is hardest for them.

on: Swami Vivekananda’s three steps: feel, think, act.

paras: "Feel, therefore, my would-be reformers, my would-be patriots! Do you feel?" Swami Vivekananda then asks whether we have found a way out, a practical solution, and whether we have the will to carry it through. In full: “You may feel, then; but instead of spending your energies in frothy talk, have you found any way out, any practical solution...? Yet that is not all. Have you got the will to surmount mountain-high obstructions?” Heart alone becomes sentimental; head alone becomes cold; hands alone become tiring. All three together make giving an art.

slides.t: Heart, head and hands in harmony
on: A diagram of three overlapping circles, heart, head and hands, with a flame where they meet: together, offered to the Lord, the whole being becomes an instrument of the Divine.
gl: love of God, which purifies the heart
unselfish work, which steadies the hands

paras: The heart feels: love and compassion, purified by devotion. The head understands: it sees the real need and plans wisely, clarified by knowledge. The hands act: steady, skilful, unselfish work, freed by offering. Where the three meet, the flame: the whole person offered to the Lord becomes an instrument of the Divine. These are the four yogas working together: bhakti for the heart, jñāna for the head, karma yoga for the hands, and meditation to gather all three. Swami Vivekananda called this harmony "my ideal of a perfect man".

on: Sri Ramakrishna’s prayer, Gītā 11.33 nimitta-mātraṁ bhava, and the image of the hollow flute.

paras: When the ego says "I am doing this", it gets in the way, like dust on a window that dims the sunlight. When heart, head and hands are offered, the "I" steps aside and the Divine works through us. Sri Ramakrishna prayed: "O Mother, Thou art the Operator and I am the machine." In the Gītā Sri Krishna tells Arjuna that the work is already done by the Lord; Arjuna has only to be the instrument. A simple practice: begin and end each task with "This is Your work; I am Your instrument." The instrument is kept clean in thought, word and deed, which we have just seen.

on: A table of sāttvika, rājasika and tāmasika offering from Gītā 17.11 to 17.13, applied to an association.
gl: quality of nature: sattva, rajas, tamas

paras: The Gītā describes yajña of the three guṇas in 17.11 to 17.13; the same applies to every act of seva, and to giving (17.20 to 17.22). The Gītā also warns of yajña done in name only, out of show, by those intoxicated with wealth and pride (16.17). These are checks for ourselves, never for judging others. Invite members to think of one recent act of service: which quality was it, and what would make it purer?

slides.t: When the ego creeps into seva
on: Five signs of ego in seva, each with its remedy, and Matthew 6:3.

paras: These are gentle checks for ourselves, never for judging others. In organisations, ego shows up as competition between groups and branches, and it quietly destroys collective work. The remedy is always the same: remember the two pillars. They are divine, and we are one. Swami Vivekananda in Karma-Yoga: "Do not stand on a high pedestal and take five cents in your hand and say, 'Here, my poor man'", "but be grateful that the poor man is there, so that by making a gift to him you are able to help yourself."

on: Gītā 12.13 with seven qualities of one dear to the Lord.

vs.dev:
अद्वेष्टा सर्वभूतानां मैत्रः करुण एव च ।
निर्ममो निरहङ्कारः समदुःखसुखः क्षमी ॥
vs.iast:
adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānāṁ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca,
nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ kṣamī
vs.en: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate to all, free from the sense of “mine” and from ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving.

paras: Gītā 12.13 to 20 is the Lord's portrait of the devotee "dear to Me". Read as a portrait of the ideal sevak: one who hates no being, is friendly and compassionate to all, is free from the sense of "mine" (nirmama) and from ego (nirahaṅkāra), stays even in pain and pleasure, and forgives. Note nirmama and nirahaṅkāra: giving up "I and mine" is exactly how the wave merges in the ocean.

on: Twelve qualities of a sevak in three rows: the heart, the character and the sevak in a team.

paras: Three rows: the heart of the sevak (love, humility, reverence, gratitude); the character of the sevak (purity, patience, perseverance, cheerfulness, echoing Swami Vivekananda's "purity, patience and perseverance... and, above all, love"); and the sevak in a team (listening, discretion, team spirit, self-care). Self-care matters: a sevak who never renews will burn out. Meditation and prayer are the fuel for seva. Invite members to choose one quality to work on this year.

slides.t: A sevak’s day: one continuous yajña
on: A diagram of the sevak’s day from dawn to night, with Gītā 9.27.

paras: The question NZICA suggested for this talk: what does a day look like in the life of a person dedicated to seva? The answer of the Gītā is 9.27: whatever you do, eat, offer, give or practise, do it as an offering to Me. The fire is lit at dawn and kept burning all day: dawn, morning practice, home, work, community, evening offering, night. The next three slides take each part in turn.

on: Five parts of the morning: on waking, prayer and meditation, a page of wisdom, the intention, and at home first.

paras: Seva is not only an event on a weekend. It begins in the morning, in the mind. A sevak who starts the day by remembering the Divine within sees the Divine more easily in others. Meditation and seva support each other: meditation fills the cup; seva pours it out.

slides.t: During the day: work as worship
on: Five parts of the day: work or study, with people, a pause, in the community, when it goes wrong. Yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam (Gītā 2.50).

paras: Yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam (Gītā 2.50): yoga is skill in action, doing work so well and so selflessly that it does not bind us. For most of us, the greatest field of seva is not a special project but our ordinary day: our job, our home, the people we meet. Real worship, as Swami Vivekananda said at Rameswaram, is seeing Shiva in them.

on: Gītā 9.27, three questions for a quiet evening review, and Holy Mother’s counsel.

vs.dev:
यत्करोषि यदश्नासि यज्जुहोषि ददासि यत् ।
यत्तपस्यसि कौन्तेय तत्कुरुष्व मदर्पणम् ॥
vs.iast:
yat karoṣi yad aśnāsi yaj juhoṣi dadāsi yat,
yat tapasyasi kaunteya tat kuruṣva mad-arpaṇam
vs.en: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in worship, whatever you give, whatever discipline you practise, O son of Kuntī, do it as an offering to Me.

paras: At the end of the day, the sevak offers everything, the successes and the failures, at the feet of the Lord. Nothing is kept as "my achievement". The evening review is gentle, not harsh: we notice where the ego came in, and resolve to do better tomorrow. Holy Mother's last advice completes the picture: when the whole world is my own, seva becomes as natural as caring for my own family. Please check the wording of Holy Mother's words against The Gospel of Holy Mother before the retreat.

on: NZICA’s third question: at the deepest level, each soul is potentially divine; together, people of Indian heritage who have made our home in Aotearoa.

paras: NZICA's third question goes to the root: who are we, what do we need to protect, and what needs to go? If we do not know who we are, we cannot know what to keep. Vedanta's answer: each soul is potentially divine; the goal is to manifest this divinity within. At Chicago Swami Vivekananda called his listeners the Children of God, the sharers of immortal bliss. Together, as members of NZICA, we are people of Indian heritage who have made our home in Aotearoa, carrying a spiritual tradition of great depth, respect for elders, love of family, hospitality, festivals, languages and the ideal of seva.

slides.t: What to protect, what to let go
on: A diagram with our true identity at the centre: on one side what to protect and nurture, on the other what to let go.

paras: The guiding principle: whatever helps to reveal the divine in us and in others is to be protected and nurtured; whatever hides it is to be let go. Protect our divine nature, dharma, gratitude and family bonds, our spiritual heritage for the young, unity and goodwill, and the spirit of seva. Let go of "I and mine", wanting credit, comparison and rivalry, resentment and old grievances, what divides us from one another, and habits that harm body and mind. A simple test for any custom, habit or attitude: does it help me and those around me to grow in love, truth and unselfishness?

on: Īśa Upaniṣad 1 with its meaning, and three cards: hold the work, the love and the ideal (Gītā 18.5); give up the grasping (18.6); Sri Ramakrishna: do all your duties, but keep your mind on God.

vs.dev:
ईशा वास्यमिदं सर्वं यत्किञ्च जगत्यां जगत् ।
तेन त्यक्तेन भुञ्जीथा मा गृधः कस्यस्विद्धनम् ॥
vs.iast:
īśā vāsyam idaṁ sarvaṁ yat kiñca jagatyāṁ jagat,
tena tyaktena bhuñjīthā mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam
vs.en: All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is to be covered by the Lord. Enjoy it by giving it up; do not covet anyone’s wealth.

paras: Enjoy by giving up does not mean leaving our homes and families; it means holding everything as the Lord's, not as "mine". The Gītā says yajña, giving and discipline are never to be given up, for they purify even the wise (18.5), but they are to be done giving up attachment and the fruits (18.6). Sri Ramakrishna's maidservant in a rich man's house performs all the household duties and brings up her master's children as if they were her own, but in her own mind she knows very well that they do not belong to her at all. He also taught that the "unripe I" that says "my house, my money, my group" is to be let go, while the "ripe I" that says "I am the servant of God, I am His child" is to be kept.

on: A diagram of many members’ offerings going into one sacred fire, with its two fruits: the good of many outwardly and the inner light within.
gl: for the good of many, for the joy of many

paras: Return to verse 2 of our theme mantra: samānena vo haviṣā juhomi, I worship with your common oblation. A collective yajña: each member brings a different offering (time, skills, knowledge, wealth, care, prayer), like the devas who each took up their own share, and all of it goes into one fire with one purpose. Outward, the fruit is bahujana hitāya, bahujana sukhāya: the good of many, the joy of many (the Buddha's words, an ideal Swami Vivekananda held up for all who serve). Inward, every member who offers is purified, and the inner light shines through. This is how NZICA becomes a powerful force for collective good.

on: Śravaṇa, manana and nididhyāsana: the talk today, the study paper and quiz, and thirty days of yajña.

paras: The talk is only the first of three steps. Śravaṇa is hearing: today. Manana is reflecting: the study paper, read one section a day, with its reflection questions and the quiz. Nididhyāsana is living it: the thirty days of yajña in Section 11 of the paper, and the seva tree note each person writes today. Branches may also study the paper together.

paras: About 15 minutes. Two or three senior members each share a short story of seva from their own lives. Keep this slide on screen while they speak.

paras: Hand out sticky notes and pens during Q&A so people are ready. Give two or three minutes of quiet to write, then invite everyone to paste their note on the seva tree as they go out to tea. A volunteer copies the Zoom chat answers onto notes. The tree stays up for the rest of the day.
